meta.title: Distributed Rate Limiter
meta.summary: Enforce per-API-key limits consistently across many gateway instances with an atomic token bucket in Redis.

functional: Limit each API key to N requests per second, with short bursts allowed
Return 429 with Retry-After when over the limit
Limits differ by plan and can change without a deploy
nonFunctional: Limits hold across all gateway instances combined
If the limiter itself fails, the API keeps serving (fail open)

slos.name: Limiter overhead
slos.sli: Limit decisions made within the threshold, divided by all decisions

slos.name: API availability with the limiter
slos.sli: Requests that succeed divided by all requests, even when the limiter is degraded

slos.name: Limit accuracy
slos.sli: Keys admitted within 5% of their configured rate, divided by all keys

alerts.when: API errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: The limiter must never be the reason the API is down.

alerts.when: Counter store p99 above 2 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: The limiter adds that latency to every request.

alerts.when: Fail-open decisions above zero for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Limits are not being enforced. Page if it lasts 15 minutes.

alerts.when: Rejection ratio for one key above 50% for 10 minutes
alerts.why: An abusive client, or a plan limit set too low for what they need.

alerts.when: Gateways running a limits table older than 5 minutes
alerts.why: Plan changes and overrides are not taking effect.

signals.name: Fail-open count
signals.why: Counts requests let through because the counter store was unreachable.

signals.name: Latency and evictions
signals.why: An evicted bucket resets a key to a full allowance.

signals.name: Allowed against rejected, by plan
signals.why: Shows whether limits match how customers really use the API.

debug.symptom: Customers get 429 responses they should not
steps: Check the limit the gateway has for that key: is the config table fresh?
Look at that key's decisions over time: a burst or sustained traffic?
Check counter store evictions and failovers: lost state changes the allowance.
Remember the Redis script uses server time, so gateway clock drift is not the cause.

flows.title: Allowed request
flows.summary: One atomic round trip to Redis decides, then the request continues to the backend.

steps.label: resolve api.example.com
steps.detail: A network load balancer has fixed IP addresses, which customers can allowlist in their firewalls. DNS answers with them and clients cache the result.

steps.label: any gateway
steps.detail: Requests from one key land on many gateways, which is why the count must be shared and not kept in local memory.

steps.label: limit for key_abc (cached)
steps.detail: Plan limits are cached in the gateway and refreshed in the background, so config is not on the hot path.

steps.label: EVALSHA token_bucket
steps.detail: A Lua script runs atomically inside Redis: refill tokens for the time elapsed, then take one. No race between gateways, one network round trip.
steps.payload:
-- KEYS[1]=tb:key_abc  ARGV: rate=100/s, burst=200, now
local t = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = math.min(burst, (t[1] or burst) + (now - (t[2] or now)) * rate)
if tokens < 1 then return {0, tokens} end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens - 1, 'ts', now)
return {1, tokens - 1}

flows.title: Throttled request
flows.summary: The bucket is empty: reject at the edge without touching the backend.

steps.label: 429 Too Many Requests
steps.detail: The backend never sees the request; rejected traffic costs almost nothing.

steps.label: 429, retry after 1 s
steps.detail: Well-behaved clients back off with jitter.

flows.title: Counter store down (fail open)
flows.summary: A limiter outage must not become an API outage.

steps.label: timeout 5 ms → local fallback
steps.detail: Fail open with a coarse local limit (key limit ÷ number of gateways). Briefly over-admitting is better than rejecting all traffic.

flows.title: Limits refresh
flows.summary: Background refresh keeps plan changes live without a deploy.

steps.label: GET limits changed since t
steps.detail: Every ~30 s each gateway pulls changes. A customer upgrade takes effect within a minute.

notes.text: Algorithms: fixed window (simple, bursty at window edges), sliding log (exact, memory-heavy), sliding window counter (good approximation), token bucket (allows controlled bursts). Token bucket is the usual pick for APIs.
Shard Redis by API key so each key's bucket lives on one shard; one round trip per request at 1M/s needs a cluster, not a single node.
Redis keeps the timestamps, so gateway clock skew does not matter. A replica promoted after failover may have slightly old counts, which is acceptable for rate limiting.
Hybrid for very hot keys: each gateway takes tokens from Redis in small batches and spends them locally, cutting Redis calls by 10× at a small cost in precision.
A network (L4) load balancer is enough here because the gateways already parse HTTP. It adds less latency, handles huge connection counts and can expose static IPs that customers allowlist.
Static IPs from the network load balancer let enterprise customers allowlist the API. Plan any IP change carefully: they cache and firewall these addresses.

questions.q: Token bucket, fixed window or sliding window: which would you choose and why?
questions.a: A token bucket allows short bursts up to a cap while enforcing an average rate, and needs only a count and a timestamp per key. Fixed windows are simpler but let a client send double the limit across a window boundary. A sliding window is the most accurate and costs more memory or computation.

questions.q: Many gateway instances update the same client's counter. How do you avoid race conditions?
questions.a: Do the check-and-decrement as one atomic operation in the counter store, for example a Lua script or an atomic increment with expiry in Redis. Reading the value and writing it back in two steps lets concurrent requests both pass. Each request costs one round trip to the store.

questions.q: The counter store goes down. Do you block all traffic or let everything through?
questions.a: Usually fail open: let requests through with a local, per-instance approximate limit, because rejecting everything turns a limiter outage into a full outage. Fail closed only for limits that protect money or security, such as login attempts. Alert either way.

questions.q: How do you keep the limiter from adding noticeable latency to every request?
questions.a: Keep the counter store close (same zone) and in memory, with one atomic call per request. For very high rates, keep local counters in each gateway and sync with the shared store in batches, accepting a small overshoot. Never call the store more than once per request.

questions.q: How do limits change per customer plan without a deploy?
questions.a: Store limits in a config store keyed by plan or customer, and have gateways cache them and refresh periodically or on a change event. Validate changes and roll them out gradually, since a bad limit can block every customer at once.

questions.q: What should a throttled client receive?
questions.a: Return HTTP 429 with headers that say the limit, how many requests remain and when to retry (Retry-After). Good clients back off using them. Return the headers on successful responses too, so clients can slow down before they hit the limit.
